question: How do BPE and unigram LM tokenization differ in the way they build their vocabularies, and which one yields subword units that line up better with morphology?

gold.quote: BPE starts from a base character set, then merges those characters based on bigram frequency to form subword units (bottom-up), whereas unigram language models start from a large subword vocabulary, which is then reduced based on a regularization method (top-down).
We observe that the unigram LM method produces subword units that qualitatively align with morphology much better than those produced by BPE.

expected_answer: BPE uses a bottom-up approach that greedily merges character pairs based on bigram frequency, while unigram language models use a top-down approach starting from a large vocabulary and iteratively pruning based on perplexity. The unigram method produces tokens that align better with morphology and recover common affixes, whereas BPE frequently absorbs affixes into adjacent units.

question: Across studies of subword vocabulary size, is a larger vocabulary always better, and what determines the best size in low-resource versus high-resource or data-constrained settings?

gold.section: 5 Results and analysis > 5.2 Analysis > 5.2.1 The impact of vocabulary size of source language
gold.quote: Additionally, we observe that a larger source language vocabulary set does not necessarily lead to better performance. This may be because the quality of the vocabulary set also affects the models' performance, which inspires us to design more precise measure to screen out a high-quality source language vocabulary set in future work.

A larger vocabulary size improves tokenization fertility, i.e., splitting sentences into fewer tokens, thereby improving the tokenization efficiency. Additionally, a larger vocabulary enables the model to capture a wider range of concept. However, the risk of under-fitting for rare tokens increases with larger vocabulary sizes, especially in the data-constrained regime.
Ding et al. (2019) explore the effect of BPE vocabulary size and find that it is better to use small vocabulary for low-resource setting and large vocabulary for a high-resource setting.

gold.section: 6 Analysis > 6.2 Effect of Vocabulary Size in Fine Tuning
gold.quote: Figure 3 shows that VA-LLM preferred large vocabulary sizes when additional target-domain monolingual data was used for training cbow, whereas it preferred small vocabulary sizes when the data was not used.

expected_answer: Multiple studies demonstrate that vocabulary size has a non-monotonic relationship with model performance. While larger vocabularies can improve tokenization efficiency and concept coverage, the optimal vocabulary size depends on computational budget, data availability, and training regime. In low-resource settings, smaller vocabularies perform better, whereas high-resource settings benefit from larger vocabularies. Additionally, vocabulary quality matters as much as size—larger vocabulary sets do not necessarily guarantee better performance.
notes: from C75 (theme1). duplicate-prone: topic shared by many papers (vocabulary size). 4 works.

question: Why do standard tokenization schemes make arithmetic hard for language models, and what number-representation or tokenization changes (such as digit-count prefixes or right-to-left tokenization) have been proposed to fix this?

gold.quote: A central limitation is that numbers are processed as symbolic tokens whose embeddings do not explicitly encode numerical value, leading to systematic errors.
Standard numeral representations do not explicitly expose digit length or place value, requiring models to infer scale implicitly during left-to-right generation.
Schwartz et al. (2024) addressed this issue by introducing a structured number format in which each numeral is prefixed with its digit count.
We find that model accuracy is up to 20% higher when using R2L tokenization (Figure 1, Section 3).

expected_answer: Standard tokenization schemes struggle with arithmetic because numbers are processed as symbolic tokens whose embeddings do not explicitly encode numerical value, and standard numeral representations do not explicitly expose digit length or place value. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed several mechanisms: introducing value-aware numerical representations that augment inputs with prefix tokens conditioned on numerical values, using structured number formats that prefix numerals with digit counts to provide early access to magnitude information, employing right-to-left tokenization instead of left-to-right to improve alignment with how arithmetic algorithms work, and incorporating regression-style signals into training objectives to encourage numerically closer predictions.
notes: from C77 (theme4). arithmetic. 2 works.

question: When adapting a tokenizer to a new language, how does replacing the least frequent existing tokens differ from appending new tokens to the vocabulary, and why can appending hurt compression?

gold.section: Appendix A Tokenizer Details > A.2 Token Replacement Details
gold.quote: In our work, instead of extending the tokenizer's vocabulary, we replace the least frequent tokens from it with tokens from the new language.
We show that this approach introduces useless tokens that do not participate in merges, resulting in lower compression compared to having tokens that are useful in tokenization.

expected_answer: Token replacement strategies keep model capacity constant by replacing the least frequent tokens with new language tokens, whereas appending strategies add new tokens to the existing vocabulary. The replacement approach avoids introducing useless tokens that don't participate in merges, resulting in better compression compared to simply appending tokens that may not be useful in the tokenization process.
notes: from C78 (theme5). tokenizer transfer. 2 works.

question: What evidence shows that the link between a tokenizer's compression rate and downstream task performance is inconsistent across studies, languages and tasks?

gold.section: 6 Related Work > 6.2 Search for Optimal Tokenization
gold.quote: In monolingual (English) models, Schmidt et al. (2024) argued that higher compression is not inherently beneficial. However, Liu et al. (2025) observed an upward trend in downstream task performance with higher compression, even when perplexity (measured in bits per byte) degraded. This discrepancy underscores the importance of evaluating downstream performance alongside language modeling metrics.

gold.section: 6 Related Work > 6.2 Search for Optimal Tokenization
gold.quote: In contrast to prior work, our extensive search reveals that the impact of compression rate on performance is non-monotonic: there exists an optimal compression rate beyond which performance degrades.

Recent work shows that better compression does not uniformly predict task performance: Lotz et al. (2025) find a statistically significant negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.59$) between compression and multiple-choice benchmark scores, and Wegmann et al. (2025) show the correlation can invert by task type.

As concrete examples, Zouhar et al. (2023) found that Rényi efficiency correlates strongly with machine translation quality, and compression rate has long been treated as the default proxy for tokenizer quality (Rust et al., 2021). Subsequent work, however, directly challenged both findings (Schmidt et al., 2024; Cognetta et al., 2024).

expected_answer: Multiple studies have found contradictory results regarding compression and downstream performance. In monolingual English models, some researchers argue higher compression is not inherently beneficial, while others observe an upward trend in downstream performance with higher compression. In multilingual settings, higher compression generally correlates with better performance, but this may reflect language frequency in training data rather than a causal relationship. Additionally, recent work has found non-monotonic relationships where optimal compression exists beyond which performance degrades, and even negative correlations between compression and benchmark scores depending on the task type.
notes: from C79 (theme6). theory / evaluation. 3 works.

question: How do the 'incomplete tokens' of byte-level BPE tokenizers differ from undertrained (glitch) tokens found by embedding-norm analysis, both in how well they were trained and in the failures they cause?

gold.quote: This is distinct from hallucinations involving glitch tokens, as previously investigated by Land and Bartolo (2024), which was attributed to undertrained tokens.

gold.section: 2 Proposed Methodology (VocabAdapt) > 2.2 Identifying Candidate Tokens for Replacement
gold.quote: The undertrained tokens are identified through the methodology of Land and Bartolo (2024) where the L2 norm for each token embedding $e_{i}$ in the vocabulary is computed, $\|e_{i}\|_{2}$, excluding partial utf-8, fallback bytes, and unreachable tokens.

expected_answer: Incomplete tokens in byte-level tokenizers are characterized by being well-trained but structurally incomplete, and they cause hallucinations distinct from those caused by undertrained tokens. Undertrained tokens, identified through low embedding norms, are vocabulary items that appeared infrequently during pretraining. While both types can cause model failures, incomplete tokens suffer from higher hallucination rates despite similar training levels to complete tokens, whereas undertrained tokens are identified by their sparse training occurrences and low embedding norms.
notes: from C80 (theme7). glitch tokens. 2 works.
